clue.text: Use intelligent anticipation to get a good seat ?

definitions.text: Use intelligent anticipation to get a good seat

parts.words: Use intelligent anticipation to get a good seat
parts.note: to act first and head off a rival; read in two words, a front stall is a prized theatre seat

explanation.surface: Advice on arriving early at the theatre to bag the best place.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the word as FORE STALL: the stalls are the ground-floor theatre seats, and those at the fore are the best.
explanation.definitionFit: To act in advance so as to prevent something is to pre-empt it, and the split reading names a front theatre seat.

parts.note: birds line their homes with soft down, and the idiom means making yourself rich

explanation.surface: Praise for some uplifting habit of birdwatchers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspiring' hides 'in' plus a sense of filling with plumes: a bird lines its home with down, and a person doing the same figuratively grows rich, often at others' expense.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to enrich oneself, taken from a bird lining its home with down.

clue.text: Make a neat collection in the direction of the circular staircase ?

definitions.meaning: to gather scattered things or animals together

definitions.text: in the direction of the circular staircase
definitions.meaning: a spiral stair goes around and upwards, so its direction is described in two words

explanation.surface: Instructions to tidy things away by carrying them up the spiral stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Gathering cattle or suspects together is the phrasal verb; a spiral staircase climbs both circling and upward.

parts.note: a dynasty of China shares its name with the past participle of a verb for performing a song

explanation.surface: A concert programme that included songs from China.
explanation.walkthrough: The Song dynasty of China was formerly spelt Sung, and the same letters say vocal music was presented, performed by voice.
explanation.definitionFit: Vocal music that has been performed has been voiced in song, and the old spelling of China's Song dynasty matches.

clue.text: "From you have I been —— in the spring" (Shakespeare)

definitions.text: "From you have I been —— in the spring" (Shakespeare)

parts.words: "From you have I been —— in the spring" (Shakespeare)
parts.note: the opening line of Shakespeare's Sonnet 98, with the word for being away left blank

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare with a word missing for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: Sonnet 98 begins 'From you have I been absent in the spring': the clue is a fill-in-the-blank quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means away or not present, the poet having been parted from the beloved.

clue.text: Aircraft component with better staying power ?

definitions.meaning: a long structural strut running the length of a fuselage
read in two words, lasting more on, holding out for a greater time

explanation.surface: A part for an aeroplane that lasts better than others.
explanation.definitionFit: A fore-and-aft spar of an airframe; split in two, it says able to stay on for more time.

definitions.meaning: two words: go on consuming food
a district of Norwich, in the English county of Norfolk

explanation.surface: Someone keeps eating while staying in Norfolk.
explanation.walkthrough: Norfolk is a county in eastern England; the place named is a suburb of its city Norwich.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep consuming a meal, said as two words; and a suburb of Norwich bears the same name.

indicators.note: the old setter lets 'in the' say that the letters of the phrase are found, reshuffled, in the answer

explanation.surface: A claim that no extras exist at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of NONE EXISTS rearrange to the answer; the signal 'in the' is weak by modern standards.
explanation.definitionFit: Annexes or added parts built onto something are things added on.

parts.note: motor-driven three-wheeled vehicles that replaced hand-pushed invalid carriages

explanation.surface: A remark on the motorised vehicles that replaced old wheeled chairs.
explanation.walkthrough: A Bath chair was a hooded wheeled chair for invalids, named after the spa town of Bath; 'powerful' means powered by an engine.
explanation.definitionFit: Early motorised three-wheelers, often used as invalid carriages, followed the hand-pushed chair.

clue.text: Novel aspect of boreal rage over a religious house

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece written over another comes first

parts.note: boreal means northern, so its compass aspect is north
rage means anger
an abbey is a monastery or convent

explanation.surface: A northern rage seems to loom above a monastery.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is Jane Austen's novel; 'over' places the religious house after the rest in a down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's Gothic parody is a book of fiction, published in 1817.

parts.note: a former pupil of a school, called an old boy in Britain

explanation.surface: A fond reference to an elderly man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old boy' is not an elderly man but a former pupil; the Latin word is used for a graduate.
explanation.definitionFit: A former student or graduate of a school or college is a past pupil.

clue.text: Trimmer, this painter, but always blue

definitions.meaning: Jean-Marc ..., French portraitist, whose name is given to a soft shade of blue

explanation.surface: A neater artist who still paints in blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean-Marc Nattier was an 18th-century French portrait painter; a blue he favoured is called by his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Smarter in dress is the comparative of a word for neat; the surname is a French portraitist's, and a blue shade.

definitions.meaning: Mr ..., the evil self of Dr Jekyll in Stevenson's story
... Park, the large royal park in central London

explanation.surface: A villain lurks in the park.
explanation.walkthrough: Hyde Park is London's large central park; Mr Hyde is Dr Jekyll's evil other self in Stevenson's tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson's villain Edward bears the name, as does London's best-known royal park.

parts.note: recalls the song '... the Arches', where homeless men dream their dreams away

explanation.surface: Asks where a fanciful person sits archly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arch' looks like the adjective for knowing, but means a bridge arch: Flanagan and Allen's song 'Underneath the Arches' has the singer dream his dreams away there.
explanation.definitionFit: Below or beneath, the position of the sleepers in the old music-hall song about railway arches.

clue.text: Sand please, well raked, for good walking surfaces

indicators.note: sand that is raked is churned up, so these letters are thoroughly mixed

explanation.surface: Asking for sand to be carefully raked for strolling on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well raked' churns SAND PLEASE into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Seafront promenades are long paved paths for strolling, often by a beach.

clue.text: Nocturnal reward for the diligent Smith

definitions.text: Nocturnal reward for the diligent Smith

parts.words: Nocturnal reward for the diligent Smith
parts.note: Longfellow's Village Blacksmith, having worked all day, has earned a night's rest

explanation.surface: A night-time prize for a hard-working man named Smith.
explanation.walkthrough: Smith is not a surname but Longfellow's Village Blacksmith: 'Something attempted, something done, / Has earned a night's repose.'
explanation.definitionFit: Rest or sleep is the earned reward at night in Longfellow's poem.

clue.text: His family tree had gay birds on it !

definitions.text: His family tree had gay birds on it

parts.words: His family tree had gay birds on it
parts.note: the Swiss Family lived in a tree house; read in two parts, red-breasted birds are perched on it

explanation.surface: A genealogy decorated with cheerful birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Family tree' is not a genealogy but the tree house of Wyss's Swiss Family; split the name ROBINS ON for the birds sitting on it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swiss Family of the novel by Wyss bears this surname, which splits as birds perched on.

parts.note: abandoned or stuck; the Strand is a London street, and a banana comes off its bunch

explanation.surface: Someone abandoned in a street named after a fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Strand is a well-known London street; to be left high and dry is to be marooned there.
explanation.definitionFit: Being left marooned or helpless, like a ship run aground on a shore.

parts.note: the highest social rank, the peerage

explanation.surface: A remark on something first-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top class' looks like an adjective for excellent but is a noun phrase, the highest social order.
explanation.definitionFit: The peerage or aristocracy is the highest social rank.

definitions.meaning: a verb: put out new growth, sprout
full of buds, read as an adjective rather than a friend

explanation.surface: An exclamation to a friend urging them to fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buddy' is not a friend but the adjective for coming into bud.
explanation.definitionFit: To sprout or begin to grow quickly; a plant doing so is putting out buds.

clue.text: "To all you ladies now at land We men at sea ——" (Lord Dorset)

definitions.text: "To all you ladies now at land We men at sea ——" (Lord Dorset)

parts.words: "To all you ladies now at land We men at sea ——" (Lord Dorset)
parts.note: the opening of the Earl of Dorset's song written at sea, with the verb for composing a letter left blank

explanation.surface: A line from an old sea song with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset, wrote the 1665 song 'To all you ladies now at land, / We men at sea indite'.
explanation.definitionFit: To write or compose a letter, the old verb the sailors use.

definitions.meaning: powdered coffee made by adding hot water
a moment, a very short time

explanation.surface: A question asking whether it's time for a coffee break.
explanation.definitionFit: Soluble powdered coffee; and a moment or split second.

parts.note: Ophioglossum is the fern genus whose name means snake's tongue, the common name being that snake's tongue

explanation.surface: Asks for the language of a botanical name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' looks like language, but the fern genus Ophioglossum is commonly called adder's-tongue; the answer fills the blank before 'tongue'.
explanation.definitionFit: The fern's common name is adder's-tongue, so the tongue belongs to the viper.

parts.note: an archaic word for young men or striplings

explanation.surface: A paradox: the young who are old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' means archaic: the answer is an old word for youths.
explanation.definitionFit: An obsolete word for lively youths or striplings.

clue.text: A touch of Islam in Angus ?

indicators.note: only part of the word Islam is taken, its first four letters

explanation.surface: A hint of Muslim influence in a Scottish place.
explanation.walkthrough: Angus is a county of eastern Scotland, through which the river runs.
explanation.definitionFit: The River Isla and Glen Isla lie in the Scottish county of Angus.

parts.note: the second Greek letter names the ray made of electrons

explanation.surface: A hint at an email message.
explanation.walkthrough: Not an email: beta rays are streams of electrons, and beta is the Greek letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The second Greek character, which names radiation consisting of electrons.

parts.note: describes a text that has been corrected and so improved

explanation.surface: A sigh of relief or approval.
explanation.walkthrough: Not an exclamation: a text that has been corrected is better.
explanation.definitionFit: A corrected, improved text has had its errors removed.

parts.note: a cherished possession, after the poor man's single young female sheep in Nathan's parable

explanation.surface: Someone's best-loved jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woolly' looks like a knitted jumper but is a young sheep; in 2 Samuel 12 the poor man's only one is his treasure, so the phrase means one's dearest possession.
explanation.definitionFit: A young female sheep, and figuratively a most treasured possession from Nathan's parable.

indicators.note: the word notes is altered, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Musical sounds made when notes are altered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being changed' rearranges NOTES.
explanation.definitionFit: Musical pitches or vocal qualities are audible noises.

parts.note: Thomas Gray wrote an ode on a far-off prospect of Eton College; coolly also means in an aloof way

explanation.surface: A grey-faced observer of the school looks on without warmth.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray is the poet Thomas Gray, author of 'Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College'; the adverb also means aloofly.
explanation.definitionFit: In an aloof, reserved manner, and from far off, as the poet saw the college.
